properties.title: Early villages grow along Cahokia Creek
properties.description: Small Late Woodland communities along Cahokia Creek preceded the later Mississippian city. The state site dates occupation from about 700 CE; its interpretive marker places these early settlements around 700–800.

properties.title: Woodhenge tracks the changing sunrise
properties.description: Successive circles of timber posts marked seasonal sunrise positions, including solstices and equinoxes. Archaeological interpretation dates the phases differently across site publications; the modern reconstruction represents one of these solar calendars.
properties.locationAccuracy: Interpretive marker by the reconstructed Woodhenge; the visible posts are a modern reconstruction, not surviving ancient timbers.

properties.title: Monks Mound rises in successive stages
properties.description: Cahokia’s builders enlarged Monks Mound through successive earth-moving stages, rather than constructing it at once. Its four terraces rose roughly 100 feet above the plain, supporting prominent buildings at the city’s center.
properties.locationAccuracy: Public interpretive marker on the Monks Mound approach; not an exact archaeological excavation or building footprint.

properties.title: Cahokia becomes a major Mississippian city
properties.description: At its peak, Cahokia supported an estimated 10,000–20,000 people. Mounds, plazas and surrounding settlements formed a large agricultural and ceremonial center linked to other communities across the region.
properties.locationAccuracy: State-site interpretive marker beside the Monks Mound parking area; a reference for the wider ancient city, not a village-house footprint.
properties.locationBasis: State-site interpretive marker beside the Monks Mound parking area; a reference for the wider ancient city, not a village-house footprint.

properties.title: A timber enclosure surrounds central Cahokia
properties.description: Residents built and repeatedly replaced a timber wall around the central precinct. Its roughly two-mile circuit and projecting bastions suggest defense as well as social separation; whether Cahokia was ever attacked is unknown.
properties.locationAccuracy: Public marker beside a reconstructed stockade section; the pin does not trace the entire ancient enclosure.
properties.locationBasis: Public marker beside a reconstructed stockade section; the pin does not trace the entire ancient enclosure.

properties.title: Cahokia’s urban population disperses
properties.description: After a long decline, Cahokia ceased functioning as a densely populated city by approximately 1350–1400. This marks a change in settlement, not the disappearance of Indigenous peoples or their descendants.
properties.locationAccuracy: State-site interpretive marker beside the Monks Mound parking area; a reference for the wider ancient city, not a village-house footprint.

properties.description: Returning from their Mississippi journey, Marquette, Jolliet and their companions traveled up the Illinois River and stopped near the present state park. Indigenous knowledge helped them understand the Mississippi’s course toward the Gulf of Mexico.

properties.description: Missionaries from Quebec established the Mission of the Holy Family beside existing Indigenous communities. The French village of Cahokia grew around the mission; it is distinct from the much older Mississippian city near Collinsville.

properties.description: After conflict over French settlement and land, Cahokia Illini moved to the Monks Mound area. A French mission chapel stood on the first terrace. Archaeology and written records document this later Indigenous occupation, centuries after the Mississippian city.

properties.description: Pierre Laclede and Auguste Chouteau established a trading settlement on the Mississippi bluff after scouting the area the previous year. River access and elevated ground supported a community whose early economy depended on trade with Indigenous peoples.

properties.description: Clement Delor established a settlement near present-day Elwood Street, initially called Louisbourg. It developed separately from St. Louis and was renamed Carondelet in 1794 under Spanish administration.

properties.description: Clark convened a council with Indigenous leaders to seek peace and weaken British alliances. Some leaders accepted an agreement while others retained their British ties; the gathering did not represent a single choice by all Native nations.

properties.description: George Rogers Clark’s Illinois campaign gained control of Cahokia, then a British-held post with a French population. Joseph Bowman’s headquarters became known as Fort Bowman, placing the village within the western theater of the American Revolution.

properties.description: Spanish soldiers and local militia defended St. Louis against a British-led attack during the American Revolution. Resistance centered on Fort San Carlos; fighting and raids extended outside the settlement.
